title: Pigeonhole and averaging arguments
terms: pigeonhole principle; generalized pigeonhole principle; residue-class pigeonholes; averag- ing principle.

exposition.text:
If N objects occupy k boxes, some box contains at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects. Equivalently, more
than k(r − 1) objects force some box to contain at least r. The proof is a counting contradiction:
if all boxes contained at most r − 1, the total could not exceed k(r − 1).
The skill is choosing boxes that encode a useful relation, such as residue classes, intervals, or
common odd parts of integers. Averaging gives complementary bounds: some box has at most
⌊N/k⌋ objects. To show a guarantee is sharp, exhibit a distribution or subset immediately be-
low the threshold that avoids the desired property.

question.text:
What is the smallest m such that every m-element subset of {1, 2, . . . , 20} contains two num-
bers, one dividing the other?
(A) 6 (B) 9 (C) 10 (D) 11 (E) 12

solution.text:
Group integers by their odd part: u, 2u, 4u, . . . for the ten odd u ≤ 20. Eleven choices force
two in one group, and the smaller divides the larger. The ten numbers 11 through 20 have
no divisibility pair, so eleven is sharp.

question.text:
What is the smallest number of integers that guarantees two have difference divisible by 17?
(A) 16 (B) 17 (C) 18 (D) 33 (E) 34

solution.text:
There are seventeen residue classes modulo 17, so eighteen integers force a repeated class.
Seventeen consecutive integers occupy distinct classes, proving that seventeen is not suffi-
cient.
